theory.intro: A **conditional probability** is the probability of one event given that another has already happened, written $P(A \mid B)$ and read '$A$ given $B$'. Knowing $B$ happened rules out everything outside $B$, so the sample space shrinks to $B$.
facts: The phrases '**given that**', '**if** … **then**', '**of**' and '**knowing that**' all signal a condition.
The event named by the condition goes **after** the bar.
For equally likely counted outcomes, $P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{n(A \cap B)}{n(B)}$, provided $n(B)>0$; working from probabilities, $P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}$, provided $P(B)>0$.
The numerator is $n(A \cap B)$, not $n(A)$, because an outcome must be in $A$ and inside the reduced sample space.
This swap is the most common mistake with conditional language.
When $A$ and $B$ are **dependent**, knowing $B$ changes how likely $A$ is.
When they are **independent** it does not, so $P(A \mid B) = P(A)$.
Give a probability as a fraction in simplest form, unless the data are decimals or percentages.
steps: Reduce the sample space to the condition.
Count the favourable outcomes inside it.

workedExamples.question_text:
The table records which team surveyed spectators support.

| | Team A | Team B | Total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Men | 84 | 56 | 140 |
| Women | 36 | 54 | 90 |
| Total | 120 | 110 | 230 |

a. Of the women surveyed, what percentage support Team B?
b. Knowing that a randomly selected spectator supports Team B, find the probability that the spectator is a woman.
workedExamples.solution_text:
a. “Of the women” restricts the sample space to the women row. There are $90$ women, of whom $54$ support Team B.
$\begin{aligned}P(\text{Team B}\mid\text{woman})&=\frac{54}{90}\\&=60\%\end{aligned}$

b. The condition restricts the sample space to the Team B column. Of its $110$ spectators, $54$ are women.
$\begin{aligned}P(\text{woman}\mid\text{Team B})&=\frac{54}{110}\\&=\frac{27}{55}\end{aligned}$

workedExamples.question_text: In a class, $28$ students study history, $19$ study chemistry and $7$ study both. A student is chosen at random. If the student studies history, what is the probability that they also study chemistry?
workedExamples.solution_text:
The condition restricts the sample space to the $28$ history students. Of these, $7$ also study chemistry.
$\begin{aligned}P(\text{chemistry}\mid\text{history})&=\frac{7}{28}\\&=\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}$

workedExamples.question_text:
For events $A$ and $B$, $P(A)=0.5$, $P(B)=0.4$ and $P(A\cap B)=0.12$. Find:
a. $P(A\mid B)$
b. $P(B\mid A)$
c. $P(A'\mid B)$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
a. The condition is $B$, so divide by $P(B)$.
$\begin{aligned}P(A\mid B)&=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}\\&=\frac{0.12}{0.4}\\&=0.3\end{aligned}$

b. The condition is $A$, so divide by $P(A)$.
$\begin{aligned}P(B\mid A)&=\frac{0.12}{0.5}\\&=0.24\end{aligned}$

c. Inside $B$, subtract the overlap with $A$ to obtain the favourable probability.
$\begin{aligned}P(A'\cap B)&=0.4-0.12\\&=0.28\end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned}P(A'\mid B)&=\frac{0.28}{0.4}\\&=0.7\end{aligned}$

workedExamples.question_text: A fair six-sided die is rolled twice. The rolls are independent. A student says, “Knowing that the first roll was a $6$, the next roll is less likely to be a $6$.” Explain the mistake and give the probability that the second roll is a $6$, given that the first was a $6$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Independent rolls do not affect each other. Knowing the first result does not change the probabilities for the second roll.
$P(\text{second roll is }6\mid\text{first roll is }6)=\frac{1}{6}$.
A previous $6$ does not make another $6$ less likely.

workedExamples.question_text:
Let $M$ mean “a club member is male” and $T$ mean “a club member prefers tennis”. Write each question in probability notation and identify which asks for a conditional probability.
a. A member is chosen from the whole club. What is the probability that the member is male and prefers tennis?
b. Of the male members, one is chosen at random. What is the probability that he prefers tennis?
c. Sam writes $P(M\mid T)$ for part b. Explain the mistake.
workedExamples.solution_text:
a. $P(M\cap T)$. Both attributes are required, and selection is from the whole club.

b. $P(T\mid M)$. This is conditional: “of the male members” restricts the sample space to $M$.

c. Sam reversed the event and condition. $P(M\mid T)$ asks whether a tennis-preferring member is male. Part b asks whether a male member prefers tennis.

workedExamples.question_text: A survey of $40$ students finds that $24$ play cricket, $18$ play soccer and $5$ play neither. One student is chosen at random. Find the probability that the student plays soccer, given that they play cricket.

foundation.question_text:
The two-way table shows the lunch orders placed at a school canteen on one day.
$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c} & \text{Year 9} & \text{Year 10} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{Hot food} & 18 & 9 & 27 \\ \text{Sandwich} & 12 & 21 & 33 \\ \hline \text{Total} & 30 & 30 & 60 \end{array}$
One order is chosen at random.
Find the probability that it is hot food, given that it was placed by a Year $9$ student, as a fraction in simplest form.
foundation.solution_text:
The condition restricts the sample space to the Year $9$ column, which has a total of $30$ orders.
Of those $30$ orders, $18$ are hot food.
$P(\text{hot food} \mid \text{Year } 9) = \frac{18}{30}$
$= \frac{3}{5}$

foundation.question_text:
The two-way table shows the lunch orders placed at a school canteen on one day.
$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c} & \text{Year 9} & \text{Year 10} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{Hot food} & 18 & 9 & 27 \\ \text{Sandwich} & 12 & 21 & 33 \\ \hline \text{Total} & 30 & 30 & 60 \end{array}$
One order is chosen at random.
Find the probability that it was placed by a Year $9$ student, given that it is hot food, as a fraction in simplest form.
foundation.solution_text:
Now the condition restricts the sample space to the hot food row, which has a total of $27$ orders.
Of those $27$ orders, $18$ came from Year $9$.
$P(\text{Year } 9 \mid \text{hot food}) = \frac{18}{27}$
$= \frac{2}{3}$

foundation.question_text:
In a class, $24$ students study history, $18$ study chemistry and $6$ study both.
One student is chosen at random.
Find the probability that they study chemistry, given that they study history, as a fraction in simplest form.
foundation.solution_text:
The condition reduces the sample space to the $24$ students who study history.
Of those $24$, $6$ also study chemistry.
$P(\text{chemistry} \mid \text{history}) = \frac{6}{24}$
$= \frac{1}{4}$

foundation.question_text:
In a group of $28$ students, $16$ play cricket, $18$ play soccer and $8$ play both.
One student is chosen at random.
Find the probability that they play soccer, given that they play cricket, as a fraction in simplest form.
foundation.solution_text:
The condition reduces the sample space to the $16$ students who play cricket.
Of those $16$, $8$ also play soccer.
$P(\text{soccer} \mid \text{cricket}) = \frac{8}{16}$
$= \frac{1}{2}$

foundation.question_text:
In a class of $30$ students, $18$ have a part-time job, $12$ catch the bus to school and $8$ both have a part-time job and catch the bus.
One student is chosen at random.
Find the probability that the student has a part-time job, given that they catch the bus, as a fraction in simplest form.

At a large school, $P(B) = 0.4$ and $P(J \cap B) = 0.15$, where $B$ is the event 'a student catches the bus to school' and $J$ is the event 'a student has a part-time job'.
Find $P(J \mid B)$ as a decimal.

development.question_text:
The two-way table shows how $60$ students travel to school and whether they have a part-time job.
$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c} & \text{Job} & \text{No job} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{Catches bus} & 14 & 22 & 36 \\ \text{Walks} & 6 & 18 & 24 \\ \hline \text{Total} & 20 & 40 & 60 \end{array}$
One student is chosen at random.
Find the probability that the student catches the bus, given that they do not have a part-time job, as a fraction in simplest form.
development.solution_text:
The condition restricts the sample space to the 'No job' column, whose total is $40$.
Of those $40$ students, $22$ catch the bus.
$P(\text{bus} \mid \text{no job}) = \frac{22}{40}$
$= \frac{11}{20}$

development.question_text:
At a large school, $30\%$ of students are left-handed.
Some students catch the bus to school.
Being left-handed is independent of whether a student catches the bus to school.
Find $P(L \mid B)$ as a percentage, where $L$ is 'the student is left-handed' and $B$ is 'the student catches the bus', and explain your answer.
development.solution_text:
The two events are independent, so knowing that a student catches the bus gives no new information about whether they are left-handed.
The reduced sample space of bus catchers has the same proportion of left-handed students as the whole school.
$P(L \mid B) = P(L)$
$= 30\%$

development.question_text:
In a population, $42\%$ of people have blue eyes, $28\%$ have blond hair and $14\%$ have both.
One person is chosen at random.
Find the probability that they have blond hair, given that they have blue eyes, to the nearest whole percentage.
development.solution_text:
The condition is 'has blue eyes', so the denominator is $42\%$.
$P(\text{blond hair} \mid \text{blue eyes}) = \frac{14}{42}$
$= \frac{1}{3}$
As a percentage, this is $33\%$ to the nearest whole percentage.

development.question_text:
A researcher surveys students about travelling to school and part-time work.
Which of these two questions is asking for a conditional probability, and which is not?
Write each one in probability notation, using $B$ for 'catches the bus' and $J$ for 'has a part-time job'.
a. A student is chosen at random from the whole survey.
What is the probability that they catch the bus and have a part-time job?
b. A student is chosen at random from those who catch the bus.
What is the probability that they have a part-time job?
development.solution_text:
a. The student is chosen from the whole survey, so the sample space is not reduced and both events must happen.
$P(B \cap J)$
This is not a conditional probability.
b. The student is chosen only from the bus catchers, so the sample space has been reduced to $B$ before the choice is made.
$P(J \mid B)$
This is the conditional probability.

development.question_text:
At a large school, $P(B) = 0.45$, $P(J) = 0.2$ and $P(J \cap B) = 0.12$, where $B$ is 'a student catches the bus to school' and $J$ is 'a student has a part-time job'.
Find $P(B \mid J)$ as a decimal.
development.solution_text:
The condition is $J$, so the denominator is $P(J)$, not $P(B)$.
$P(B \mid J) = \frac{P(J \cap B)}{P(J)}$
$= \frac{0.12}{0.2}$
$= 0.6$

development.question_text:
The two-way table shows the lunch orders placed by $80$ students at a school canteen.
$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c} & \text{Year 8} & \text{Year 9} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{Hot food} & 15 & 21 & 36 \\ \text{Sandwich} & 25 & 19 & 44 \\ \hline \text{Total} & 40 & 40 & 80 \end{array}$
One order is chosen at random.
Find the probability that it was placed by a Year $9$ student, given that it is a sandwich, as a fraction in simplest form.
development.solution_text:
The condition restricts the sample space to the sandwich row, whose total is $44$.
Of those $44$ orders, $19$ came from Year $9$.
$P(\text{Year } 9 \mid \text{sandwich}) = \frac{19}{44}$

mastery.question_text:
The two-way table shows a survey of $80$ students.
$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c} & \text{Bus} & \text{No bus} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{Job} & 18 & 6 & 24 \\ \hline \text{No job} & 42 & 14 & 56 \\ \hline \text{Total} & 60 & 20 & 80 \end{array}$
One student is chosen at random. Find $P(\text{bus} \mid \text{job})$ and $P(\text{job} \mid \text{bus})$ as fractions in simplest form.
mastery.solution_text:
1. **Reduce the sample space to the condition**
For $P(\text{bus} \mid \text{job})$, the condition is 'has a part-time job', giving a reduced sample space of $24$ students.
For $P(\text{job} \mid \text{bus})$, the condition is 'catches the bus', giving a reduced sample space of $60$ students.
2. **Count the favourable outcomes inside it**
Both calculations count the same $18$ students in the top-left cell.
3. **Write the fraction and simplify**
$P(\text{bus} \mid \text{job}) = \frac{18}{24}$
$= \frac{3}{4}$
$P(\text{job} \mid \text{bus}) = \frac{18}{60}$
$= \frac{3}{10}$

mastery.question_text:
At a large school, $P(B) = 0.6$ and $P(J \cap B) = 0.15$, where $B$ is 'a student catches the bus to school' and $J$ is 'a student has a part-time job'.
Find $P(J' \mid B)$ as a decimal.
mastery.solution_text:
The condition is $B$, so the denominator is $P(B) = 0.6$.
Inside $B$, the favourable students are those without a part-time job, so subtract the overlap from $P(B)$.
$P(J' \cap B) = 0.6 - 0.15$
$= 0.45$
$P(J' \mid B) = \frac{0.45}{0.6}$
$= 0.75$

mastery.question_text:
In a survey of $36$ students, $21$ catch the bus to school, $15$ have a part-time job and $6$ do neither.
One student is chosen at random.
Find the probability that the student has a part-time job, given that they catch the bus, as a fraction in simplest form.
